extra.message: The login query is built by string formatting the `username` and `password` values that come straight from the login form (bad/mod_user.py:16-20). A password such as `' OR '1'='1` authenticates as the first user in the table, and the injection also allows arbitrary read of the users table (UNION). Use parameterised queries.

Authentication is delegated to libuser.login(), which concatenates the submitted username/password into the SQL WHERE clause. An attacker can bypass authentication entirely (e.g. username `admin' -- `) and obtain a session for any account, including admin.

User registration builds the INSERT statement with %-formatting of the attacker-supplied username and password from /user/create (bad/mod_user.py:45-52). A quote in either field breaks out of the string literal and allows arbitrary SQL to be executed against db_users.sqlite.

The UPDATE statement interpolates the new password (from the /user/chpasswd form) and the username directly into SQL. A payload like `x' WHERE 1=1 -- ` rewrites every user's password, giving full account takeover.

user_create() builds the INSERT with %-formatting of `username` instead of a bound parameter, unlike every other query in this module. Any caller passing an attacker-controlled username injects SQL into db_users.sqlite.
The seed INSERT is assembled with %-formatting of user/password values rather than parameter binding, an unsafe query-construction pattern that breaks as soon as the seed data is externally sourced.
The users table is populated with a %-formatted INSERT statement instead of parameterised values, an unsafe SQL construction pattern.

The session cookie is just base64(JSON({'username': ...})) with no signature, MAC or encryption. Any client can craft `vulpy_session` = base64 of {"username": "admin"} and be treated as that user by every route that reads g.session, a complete authentication bypass.

extra.message: API-key authentication is performed by using the raw X-APIKEY header as a filesystem glob pattern. Sending `X-APIKEY: *` (or `?*`) matches the first existing key file and authenticates the attacker as that user without knowing any key. The header must be compared literally against a stored secret.

The `username` value taken from the /api/key JSON body is embedded in a glob pattern and every match is unlinked. A username containing path separators and traversal (e.g. `../../home/user/x`) makes the glob resolve outside /tmp, so an unauthenticated request can delete attacker-chosen files. The name is never canonicalised or allowlisted.

extra.message: The key file path is built by formatting the client-supplied `username` into '/tmp/vulpy.apikey.{}.{}' and then touched. A username containing `../` escapes /tmp and lets a remote caller create empty files at arbitrary filesystem locations writable by the server process.

extra.message: The API key itself is stored as part of a filename in the shared, world-readable /tmp directory. Any local user can list /tmp and read every user's live API credential.

extra.message: /user/chpasswd has no authentication guard (compare bad/mod_posts.py:27 and bad/mod_mfa.py:38, which check `'username' not in g.session`). It changes the password of whatever username appears in the forgeable session cookie, so combined with bad/libsession.py:6 anyone can reset any account's password.

The password change flow never asks for or verifies the current password before calling libuser.password_change(). Anyone with a hijacked session or a CSRF-able browser session can permanently take over the account. The hardened variant does verify it (good/mod_user.py:73).

This state-changing POST handler has no CSRF token validation, and the app registers no CSRF middleware (bad/vulpy.py:44-52 only loads the session). A cross-site form submission silently changes the victim's password. The same gap affects /user/create and /posts/.
MFA is disabled by an unprotected GET request with no CSRF token and no re-authentication. Any cross-origin resource (e.g. ) strips the second factor from a logged-in victim's account.

The only CSRF defence on the MFA-disable action is an equality check on the Referer header, still on a GET request. Referer is attacker-influenceable (and often absent/stripped), so this is not an effective anti-CSRF control; a synchronizer token on a POST is required.

Post text submitted by users (bad/mod_posts.py:33 and /api/post) is rendered with the `| safe` filter, disabling Jinja2 autoescaping. Any user can store `<script>` in a post and execute it in every viewer's browser; because /posts/<username> is public and the session cookie has no HttpOnly flag, this yields session theft.
The hardened template still renders user-submitted post text through `| safe`, bypassing autoescaping and allowing stored XSS.
Flashed messages are rendered with `| safe`, so any message that ever incorporates request data (usernames, error text) becomes an XSS sink. Autoescaping should not be disabled on message output.

The application is started with debug=True, enabling the Werkzeug interactive debugger. Any unhandled exception exposes source code, local variables and an in-browser Python console that grants remote code execution as the server user.
The SSL entry point also runs with debug=True, exposing the Werkzeug debugger console (remote code execution) and full tracebacks.
The hardened variant is also launched with debug=True, leaving the Werkzeug debugger and verbose tracebacks active.
The Flask SECRET_KEY is hardcoded to the trivially guessable value 'aaaaaaa'. Anyone who knows it can forge signed Flask session cookies and flash messages.
SECRET_KEY is hardcoded to 'aaaaaaa' in the SSL entry point, allowing forgery of any value signed with the app secret.
The Flask SECRET_KEY is committed in source rather than loaded from the environment or a secret store; the checked-in value must be treated as public and permits session-cookie forgery.

The HS256 JWT signing secret is hardcoded as 'MYSUPERSECRETKEY' and used both to issue (line 20) and verify (line 45) API tokens. Knowledge of this repo lets an attacker mint valid bearer tokens for any username, fully bypassing API authentication.

The Fernet key that encrypts and authenticates session cookies is hardcoded in source. With this key an attacker can forge a session token for any username, defeating the session-integrity protection entirely.

Default account credentials ('admin'/'SuperSecret', 'elliot'/'123123123', 'tim'/'12345678') are hardcoded in the initialisation script and inserted verbatim, so every deployment ships with known, weak admin credentials.
The hardened initialiser also hardcodes default account passwords ('admin'/'SuperSecret' and two weak numeric passwords), giving every deployment predictable credentials.

Passwords are written to the users table in cleartext, and authentication compares them literally (bad/libuser.py:12), as does registration (bad/libuser.py:25) and password change (bad/libuser.py:53). Any read of db_users.sqlite — including via the SQL injection in the same module — discloses every user's password.
